approachQuestion.prompt:
Street markers

A nondecreasing array x lists locations requiring a painted strip. One strip may be placed anywhere on the line and covers a closed segment of length L. Return the minimum number of strips covering every location. Strips may overlap; duplicate locations are allowed.

Example 1: x=[1,2,6,7,10], L=3 → 3. Segments [1,4], [6,9], [10,13] suffice.
Example 2: x=[2,2,5], L=3 → 1; endpoints are covered.

Constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 200000; 0 ≤ x[i] ≤ 10^9; 1 ≤ L ≤ 10^9; x is already sorted. Input is read-only. Return only the stated scalar result. All arithmetic and comparisons use constant-time exact 64-bit operations; all intermediate values fit.

options.text: Scan left to right. At the first uncovered coordinate p, add one strip [p,p+L] and skip all coordinates it covers.
options.feedback: Any cover must cover the leftmost uncovered point p. Moving that covering strip so its left end is p loses no required point on the left and reaches at least as far right. Repeat on the remaining suffix.

options.text: Center a strip on each first uncovered coordinate and skip the coordinates it covers.
options.feedback: Centering wastes available reach on the empty left side. For x=[0,3] and L=3 it uses two strips although [0,3] uses one.

options.text: Return the ceiling of (last coordinate minus first coordinate) divided by L, with a minimum of one for nonempty input.
options.feedback: Span alone does not measure the required cover. For x=[0,100] and L=1 the formula returns 100, but two strips suffice; empty input should return zero.

options.text: Enumerate every legal sequence of decisions, evaluate each complete candidate, and return the best result.
options.feedback: Exhaustive search can find the right result, but revisits combinations of decisions that the safe local rule resolves directly. The number of candidates grows far beyond what the input limit permits.

Place a covering strip at the first uncovered marker. Moving its start farther left cannot cover any still-needed marker earlier, and only shortens its right reach. Then skip every marker covered by its inclusive end.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed frontier method, regardless of your previous choice. Use exactly the frontier method above as iterative scans with scalar indices, counters and accumulators. Do not copy the input and do not store a decision list. Let n be the number of input records or positions. Choose the tightest standard worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Input and returned scalar are excluded. All other live storage, including copying and any call stack, is counted. No hashing or expected-time operations are used.

feedback.reason: Each sorted marker is inspected and skipped at most once.

messages.text: The method stores no per-item history or copied input.
The scans do not restart for each item.
In the worst case every input item can affect the answer.

details: Each marker is consumed once by the forward scan, even when one strip skips many markers, giving O(n) worst-case time. The current uncovered coordinate, strip end, index, and count are fixed scalar state, so auxiliary space is O(1).
“Time O(n), auxiliary space O(n)”: The method stores no per-item history or copied input.
“Time O(n²), auxiliary space O(1)”: The scans do not restart for each item.
“Time O(1), auxiliary space O(1)”: In the worst case every input item can affect the answer.
